items.label: No. 138
items.sum: Gloomy report of Belgrave's 11th place in the National London-Brighton relay, never higher than tenth, won by Derby and County.
items.s: NATIONAL LONDON-BRIGHTON RELAY - APRIL 11TH. Gloomy report of Belgrave's 11th place in the National London-Brighton relay, never higher than tenth, won by Derby and County. The report on this race can usually be made interesting but how can anyone raise enthusiasm over a team which at no time during the whole race was higher than tenth and at one stage was as far back as sixteenth? The tale of woe really began during the week prior to the race when firstly John Davies was forced to withdraw because of foot trouble and then Clive Shippen contracted enteritis and had to stand down. John had been allocated the first leg and this was given to Charlie Walker who could not, this year, impress the selectors sufficiently to gain more than the first reserve designation. A quick switch of Eric Gebbett from the fifth to the fourth leg let in Jim Masters on the Redhill stage which has almost become his own property by divine right. The race started in fine weather but soon after Purley was passed ( we joined the race at this well known place as our Cross-Country Secretary resides there!) it began to rain. Our spirits were at a very low ebb on finding our team back in 13th place, and the weather did nothing to improve them. They were raised subsequently, for brief intervals, at the prospect of a position in the first half of the field! The whole story is most dismal; Charlie Walker struggled into tenth place on the first leg in a poor time, Malcolm Robinson floundered along on the second and lost three places, his time of 26.18 being the fifteenth best of the day, and Colin Collis,who was entrusted with the vital stage from Mitcham to Purley after his brilliant run in the T.V.H. relay, had an almost complete breakdown and finished in a distressed condition in 15th place. At this point we were 3m.42s. behind Coventry Godiva who were then leading. We now hoped that Eric Gebbett would redeem our fate but this was not to be and we remained in the same position but dropped to 4m.24s. behind the leaders, Derby and County, who were never again to be headed. Even Jumbo Masters could do nothing to put the matter right and fell back to 16th with a gap of 5m.55s. between us and Derby. Truly a hopeless position but Alan Black set out to prove that his loss of form over the previous few weeks was purely temporary and with the fifth fastest time of the day brought us back to 14th. Archie Bedford, although on the wrong side of forty, put up a plucky effort across Gatwick Aerodrome and, despite being forced to give way to Shaftesbury, can be said to have run true to form. Pat Newell must have been very dispirited waiting for well over six minutes after the leaders had passed by for his turn to come and this obviously affected his performance, for he could make no impression on those ahead and remained in fourteenth place. Next came Dave Baulch, making his last appearance for Belgrave (so he says), and he set off as though he really meant Belgrave to reach Brighton first. Running with more zest than most of the team put together he whipped past two of the opposition and took us to twelfth. Bhatia, on his first, and we sincerely hope not his last Brighton, took over in cold, wet and dreary conditions far from suitable for his type of running and, with a very good effort, he gained one more place. John Moore could make no more progress and Brian Hallowell on the last stage was over two minutes behind the team in front and could do no more than maintain his position despite a time which was the fourth fastest of the day. Inquests gain nothing but it is evident we must look for new faces before the October race for Southern Clubs. On this showing I would forecast that only Alan Black, Dave Baulch, Renjit Bhatia and Brian Hallowell will retain their places in the team - I wonder how right I shall be. items.s: CLUB 20 MILES WALK CHAMPIONSHIP - APRIL 18TH Report of the club 20 miles walk championship, led from the start by Eric Hall, with Cyril Yescombe third in a big personal best. Perverse Mother Nature was in a cold and boisterous mood when our walkers faced the starter for the 20 miles Championship. Once again we welcomed some visitors from the Met. Police A.C. in the field of eighteen starters. Eric Hall went into the lead immediately, accompanied by Terry Clark who only completed two laps of the course. Halfway times were not outstanding; Eric and Terry Clark were still leading with Ray Hall in 3rd place closely followed by Cyril Yescombe and George Beecham who were about three minutes in front of George Checkley. Johnny Morris was walking a very steady race but one or two of the back men were travelling too fast and suffered from the cold in the later stages of the race. Over the last five miles George Beecham dropped back to fifth place after an unhappy time but Cyril Yescombe held on to third place and, having walked his fastest 10 miles in the first part of the race, completed the course in a very fast time which was over 10 minutes better than he had ever done before. This split the handicap wide open and Cyril treated us to an even bigger and better grin. Johnny Morris's steady walking (20 miles at an almost identical speed each mile) gave him second handicap prize. Eric improved on the previous best time for the race on this course by over twenty seconds and gained third handicap prize. And so to Imber Court with a true Belgravian effort for the 'National 20'. items.sum: Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary, greetings from 1899 Hon. Secretary F.A. Bool, news of Len Fletcher in hospital, thanks to Frank Simmons for winter coaching, and a call to support the Track Championships at Hurlingham.
items.s: FROM THE HON. SECRETARY Hon. Secretary's notes: Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary, greetings from 1899 Hon. Secretary F.A. Bool, news of Len Fletcher in hospital, thanks to Frank Simmons for winter coaching, and a call to support the Track Championships at Hurlingham. It is with considerable pleasure that we advise the appointment of Les Stokell as Junior Hon. Secretary.His address is:- 174, Frant Road, Thornton Heath, Surrey, and all our junior members are asked to record this address on their summer fixture card, and make themselves known to Les at the earliest opportunity. He will, of course, work in close cooperation with other Club officers; and we expect, under Les Stokell's guidance, to see the younger element in the Club progressively go from success to success. Les is probably the ideal man for the job he has undertaken. As a schoolmaster he will know the problems of the younger member, as a qualified Physical Training Instructor he is in a position to advise and assist on many athletic problems. As a former member of our teams and as an International runner (he represented Canada at the Vancouver Empire Games) Les has a lot of knowledge to impart and experience to pass on; as a strong personality with tremendous enthusiasm and competence he can well become one of the greatest assets Belgrave have ever had. We were pleased to have greetings and good wishes recently from Mr. F.A. Bool, a Life Member, who became Hon. Secretary of the Club in 1899, and succeeded A.H.N. Edwards who had occupied this position for the first twelve years of the Club's existence. Mr Bool recalls the early racing, including sprints, on the Embankment. Still resident in Chelsea he follows the Club's activities with the greatest interest. Len Fletcher, one of our great walkers from 1925 onwards, is again in West Middlesex Hospital; but it is now hoped that a new course of treatment will bring almost complete recovery. We sincerely hope so and send Len all good wishes. Congratulations and thanks to Frank Simmons on the success of the winter coaching and training sessions at Chelsea Barracks. No doubt the hard work done there will be reflected in better performances than ever before on the track this coming season. Very special attention is called to our Track Championships on Saturday June 6th at HURLINGHAM PARK TRACK, S.W.6 and it is hoped that every Club member will come along and bring his friends. There is ample accommodation for all. It is hoped also that our athletes will show their appreciation of an excellent track and first class arrangements and give us bumper entries in all events, and keenly fought out Championships. Hurlingham Track is easily reached from Putney Bridge Station (District Line), and many bus routes run nearby. There is ample car parking accommodation at the track. Let's make this a really memorable occasion! Les Stokell Les Stokell appointed Junior Hon. Secretary; schoolmaster and PT instructor; represented Canada at the Vancouver Empire Games F.A. items.label: No. 138
items.sum: The cross-country secretary's review of a disappointing 1958/9 winter season for Belgrave, race by race, with a call for modern training and a revival of club spirit.
items.s: CROSS COUNTRY SECRETARY'S NOTES The cross-country secretary's review of a disappointing 1958/9 winter season for Belgrave, race by race, with a call for modern training and a revival of club spirit. These notes will reach you well after the end of the cross-country season but I hope you will forgive me for recapping on the winter activities. To say that the overall results were disappointing is putting it mildly. At the beginning of September I was hopeful that 1958/9 would start a revival for Belgrave and we would recover some of our lost glory but the Surrey Road Relay at Woking found us taking a back seat behind Herne Hill, Walton and South London. The following week we took part in the Polytechnic Relay (8 x 3 miles) and it was encouraging to finish three complete teams. The 'A' team were fifth, the 'B' team were ninth for which they qualified for the medals awarded to the first 'B' team, and the 'C' team twenty-fifth. Good times were recorded by Baulch, Bhatia, Davies and Newell. These two races,followed by our own 5¾ miles road race and 3 miles yacht handicap, preceded the London to Brighton Relay for Southern clubs on October 11th and we had every reason to think we were set for a place - in actual fact we had to struggle hard to secure sixth place to qualify for the National Relay in April. On October 25th we revisited Chelmsford for their annual relay after an absence of some years. A strong team,on paper,took eighth place, 2½ minutes behind Woodford. A cross-country relay at Reigate Priory on November 1st gave us seventh place with minor clubs like Deptford Park, Brighton, Hercules and Rochester ahead of us. On November 22nd we lost our hold on the L.C.C. Championship, taking third place behind Highgate and Queens Park Harriers. Charlie Walker and John Moore did well to take 8th and 10th places respectively. The first major cross-country race, the South of the Thames Junior, was held at Epsom Downs on November 8th and Ken Miller(20th), John Moore(26th), Malcolm Robinson(34th) and Clive Shippen(35th) ran well to give us 3rd team award behind South London and Walton. For the next two months we engaged in inter-club fixtures with reasonable success and also held our 7 miles Championship in which Charlie Walker caught Pat Newell on the wrong foot and, against the form book, chalked up another win in this race. The first Saturday in January is always set aside for the county championships and this year the Surrey race was held at Epsom Downs. Although we packed well together we could do no better than fifth, with South London, Herne Hill, Walton and Surrey A.C. taking the earlier positions. Malcolm Robinson was unfortunately forced to retire when well placed, thus depriving us of a possible place. The 10 miles Championship on January 24th reversed the result of the "seven" and gave Pat Newell an easy win over Walker with John Moore again taking third place. Eight minutes covered the first twelve runners, a very wide spread and not very encouraging for the big championships to follow in February and March. The first of these was the South of the Thames Senior which was held from our own headquarters at short notice owing to extensive flooding at the planned venue at Maidenhead. This is a race which we have won on a number of occasions and most of our leading runners are ineligible. Nevertheless our twelfth position was far from satisfactory over our own familiar terrain. The winning team Portsmouth, finished seven men before our first runner, John Moore, who was 49th, and South London, who were second, placed six men in front of John! On February 14th we travelled to Aylesford for the Southern and were surprised by the much improved running of our team which took fifth place with 345 points after T.V.H.(169), Woodford(208), Portsmouth(283) and S.L.H.(305). It was grand to see the lads making steady progress throughout the race - another five miles would probably have secured us a place! Special mention should be made of Pat Newell who took 14th position in very good company - a great effort. Three weeks later the National was held from the Hotpoint Factory at Peterborough but the hope of a good position, after our improved form in the Southern, did not materialize and we scored a record number of points - 980. Let the individual positions speak for themselves - Newell 59th, Shippen 136th, Baulch 158th, Gebbett 174th, Bedford 205th and Walker 248th. The annual visit to Ilford for the local club's relay followed the National by seven days and produced second place behind Woodford Green who beat the course record with 3h.4m.42s. Our time of 3h.6m.25s. is the second best we have shown over this course. Strangely enough it was five years ago when we caned the record to win in 3h.6m.1s. - is this a reflection on our present strength when times generally are much faster? On March 21st we held our road Championship and Pat Newell added yet another victory to his ever growing list of Club Championships with a record breaking run of 28m.21s. Dave Baulch took second place and Malcolm Robinson was third. We visited Cranford for the T.V.H. road relay on Easter Saturday and started four teams but were without a number of our best performers, and in consequence were not in the running for leading honours. The 'A' team were 8th, the 'C' team 12th and the 'D' team 15th. Colin Collis, in a welcome return to form, produced the fastest time of our boys. The last effort of the winter season is the National Relay over the London to Brighton course. Our team on paper appeared to be our best for some years, but again we were to be greatly disappointed and, after much floundering in the lower half of the field, we could do no better than 11th for the second year in succession, some nine minutes behind the winners, Derby and County A.C. Now we have to qualify in the race for Southern clubs in October in order that the "Claret and Gold" shall be seen on the Brighton road next April. Thus the season came to an end on a despondant note and my hopes of six months earlier had not been realised, A few bright specks in the shape of the Southern and the Ilford relay, in an otherwise dark sky indicate that our prospects may not be as poor as they would appear. In fact I know that our past glories will return, but not before we have all taken complete stock of ourselves. Athletes and Officials alike must change their ideas. Obviously a club having a membership such as ours must again come to the fore, but if this is to be accomplished we must discard obsolete methods of training which produce a general fitness but do not bring the speed and strength required for the modern level of athletics. Circuit training and regular exercises with the weights must become standard to the schedules of everyone, not just the few. This combined with longer and more varied running sessions, a la Herb Elliott, will ensure faster times and increased confidence. It only needs an average improvement of 45 seconds per man for us to again win a Brighton relay and to reduce our National score by over 500 points. This improvement is well within the capabilities of many of our runners and with the advent of our leading juniors such as Alan Black, Ken Miller, Chris Thompson, Alan Peckings and Derek Crookes, to mention just a few, in to senior competition with, I hope, the return of such performers as George Flanagan, Charlie Dabbs and Ron Linstead, I look to the future with considerable anticipation. If small clubs like Derby, Sheffield and Portsmouth and clubs like South London and Thames Valley who are no larger than ourselves can do well then so can we. Therefore I want you all to analyse your training methods to see where you went wrong - set yourself an improved target and don't give up until it is attained. Use Club events throughout the year to achieve your ambition and don't be sidetracked by other subsidiary interests. Remember that in trying to put Belgrave back on the map you yourself may also attain honours and I can assure you that there is nothing more satisfying than winning your county colours as a prelude to representative and International recognition. A revival of that pre-war spirit which took a small group of our members to team and individual honours, in combination with a greater attention to training, will produce the results which, I am sure, are not far away. Why not start now to build up that spirit by getting together with other members and resolving to become Belgravians whose names will be added to that select roll of "never to be forgottens". A sense of friendly rivalry will do much to gain this object - go to it!! Baulch Baulch 158th National Bhatia Bhatia Davies Davies Newell Newell 59th National Charlie Walker Charlie Walker 8th L.C.C. items.sum: Track secretary Dave Shepherd urges members to support all club fixtures and keep in touch with section officials.
items.s: TRACK SECRETARY'S NOTES Track secretary Dave Shepherd urges members to support all club fixtures and keep in touch with section officials. Members should by now have received their fixture cards for the track season and it is hoped that all concerned will note that they are expected to support all Club fixtures - it is, in fact, an obligation. I would like to point out that these fixtures do not arrange themselves, but that a vast amount of work is put in by Section Secretarys, Captains and Vice Captains to make a coherent programme. If you have any queries, get in touch with your section Secretary, Captain or Vice Captain. Don't wait for them to come to you - go to them. Tell them what you are doing in training or what you mean to do. They can only help you if you help yourself. All the best! Dave Shepherd Dave Shepherd Dave Shepherd

items.sum: The outgoing editors' farewell editorial, thanking contributors and praising the coaching of the club's youngsters.
items.s: EDITORIAL The outgoing editors' farewell editorial, thanking contributors and praising the coaching of the club's youngsters. Dear Fellow Members, In all probability this is the last Belgravian editorial which will flow from this pen, for it is hoped that new editors will take over the magazine after September. We feel that our contribution over the last few years, though small, has helped to ensure the recording of Club activities, successes and failures, and, we trust, in a manner and vein acceptable to most. We have not pleased everyone all of the time and have not been immune from personal attack (once for something we didn't even write!). But the magazine is there for everyone to air his views and the greater the interest of any individual in Club affairs the more eager he becomes to expound his theories and invite criticism. And what better way than through the Belgravian? We are indebted to Clive Shippen for his well prepared reports, to Alf Harley, whose knowledge of Club history is second to none and whose writings are always of such great interest, and to all those members whose contributions have enabled us to produce the magazine during our term as editors. It is our hope that even greater support will be extended to the new editors. In passing we must pay tribute to the great efforts being made by Les Stokell and Tom Carter in recruiting and training the fine band of youngsters who are now so successfully performing in Belgrave colours. Here lies our chance to build future teams of National class and we ask that all members, old and young, see to it that the necessary words of encouragement are given to these lads; we all know what it means to be noticed "by those who matter". items.s: HON. SECRETARY'S NOTES The Hon. Secretary's notes: a timekeeping qualification for E.T. Ryan, a visit from Wally Bayliss, Jack Bidgood's M.B.E., an athletics clinic introduced by Don Brown, and tickets for the White City Floodlit Meeting. We congratulate our Vice-President E.T. Ryan on qualifying to be added to the list of First-grade Timekeepers. He is a very worthy addition and we count ourselves fortunate on having his services and of our ever-reliable Dick Savage. How nice to see our former President, and Hon. Secretary for 11 years, Wally Bayliss, at one of our evening meetings recently. Welly was a great figure in our Club life for many years and his wager (hush!) of a pound to a penny on Belgrave when they held a commanding lead in the Brighton Relay, which was lost in the last few yards, has become one of the Club legends. Let's see you again soon, Wally! Congratulations to Vice-President Jack Bidgood on the award of the M.B.E. in the Queen's Birthday Honours List. We know it to be well deserved. We have had the very good fortune to be introduced to a private Athletics Clinic in the Knightsbridge area, equipped with the most modern apparatus and staffed by qualified physiotherapists with a very deep interest in our sport. Already one of our Olympic athletes has had successful curative treatment of an injury and other prominent members have received the benefit of the most modern treatments at nominal cost. We are indebted to our former Champion and member of many years standing, Don Brown, for this valuable introduction; and any members who feel they would benefit from the facilities available should, in the first instance, contact Don at Kensington 3336 for an appointment to be made. Our Club benefits financially each year from the promotion of the Floodlit Meeting (this year on Sept. 30th) at the White City. You will help yourself athletically by witnessing one of the finest meetings of the season - as this promotion always is; and you will be assisting our Club and many others that we meet in sporting rivalry if you go along. Tickets at all prices may be booked through Frank Webb, 50 Longford Avenue, Southall, Middx., but it must be done quickly. E.T. Ryan E.T. items.sum: Report of Belgrave's depleted team finishing 5th of eleven clubs at the Sward Trophy meeting at Chiswick, won jointly by L.A.C. and T.V.H.
items.s: SWARD TROPHY MEETING Report of Belgrave's depleted team finishing 5th of eleven clubs at the Sward Trophy meeting at Chiswick, won jointly by L.A.C. and T.V.H. May 9th brought round "The Sward" once again at Chiswick. On paper our team was, I think, the strongest we have ever been able to enter, but injuries, illness and other matters seriously depleted it. As we have no really adequate reserves we were unable to supply competitors in the 120 yds. hurdles, Pole Vault, Discus or High Jump. Tolson had pulled a muscle, Norman Caves had contracted tonsilitis, Andorka was sitting very important exams and Mal Ash threatened to retire; I was unable to change his mind. However, those who did turn out put up some fine performances and I am sure that, with the help of our absentees, we could have troubled L.A.C. and T.V.H. who tied for the trophy. Percy Porter gave us a good start with 4th place in the hammer (155'9"), Derek McCorquindale, in his first outing for Belgrave, showed his class and won the shot with 49'0¼" and our Captain Dave Ansell took second place in the long jump with 21'4½" and, deputising for Norman Caves, 5th in the triple jump at 42'3½" (a personal best). Charlie Jones had his first outing over the 440 yds. hurdles and was 5th in 58·8s. He is bound to improve a lot on this with more competition and increased confidence. John Sams, who last year won the A.A.A. Junior 200 yds. hurdles, was running for the first time as a senior in the 220 yds. hurdles. I am sure he was disappointed at not reaching the final but National Service and shortage of training took their toll. Next year perhaps a win! We also had Alan Black running only his second steeplechase as a senior. Unfortunately he bruised a heel on the third lap when landing from a hurdle and was forced to change his hurdling leg but with true Belgrave spirit he kept going and finished a very creditable 6th in 9m.53·7s. John Ware was our javelin man and he threw up to his early season form but 158'4" was not good enough for a place in that class of competition. We scored 19 points for 5th place out of eleven clubs. As usual there were some relays and running events for which we had invitations. Our 4 x 110 yds. team failed to materialize and in the 4 x 440 yds. we were fifth. Frank Wright, Pat Fox, Alan Jackson and Brian Morris constituted our team. The medley relay saw us finish in 6th place. We had only three men in the two miles team race and finished well down but Malcolm Robinson ran a personal best of 9m.24s. to finish seventh. C.J. items.sum: History of Belgrave's performances in the News of the World London to Brighton relay (later the National Relay) and the Southern Relay from 1924 to 1959, signed A.A.H.
items.s: BELGRAVE AND BRIGHTON RELAYS - 1924 to 1959 History of Belgrave's performances in the News of the World London to Brighton relay (later the National Relay) and the Southern Relay from 1924 to 1959, signed A.A.H. The first relay race on the Brighton road organised by the "News of the World" took place in 1924. Belgrave did not merit an invitation to compete on this occasion and sixteen clubs, all Southern, took part with Surrey A.C. proving the winners in 4hrs. 50min.0·2s. Each competing club fielded a team of ten men. In the following year, Belgrave were still absentees, but Birchfield Harriers entered for the first time and proved equal to their great reputation by winning from a field of seventeen teams. In 1926 we received an invitation to compete, following a qualifying race, and Hallamshire Harriers from the North were also in the field for the first time. We were never conspicuous at any time; seventh position at Merstham was our best, and at Brighton we were 14th. On the ninth stage (then 5 miles 486 yds. up Dale Hill) Bert Footer returned second fastest time. In 1927 we again qualified, but in the relay itself we suffered grave disappointment for we were never nearer than ninth, and eventually finished 17th. Our one small mead of satisfaction was the running of A.E. Smith whose time on the Mitcham to Purley stage was third fastest. In 1928 we were (not unexpectedly!) called on to qualify in a trial race once again, and this we did in emphatic fashion, winning the trial by over two minutes. In the Brighton Relay itself we managed to improve by 11½ minutes on our time of the previous year and finished 12th in the race. We were never higher than 10th and never lower than 14th throughout; and derived satisfaction from our evident solidarity even if brilliance was lacking. 1929 marked a turning-point and gave us our first set of medals in this race. For the first time we included in our team Arthur Allum and Arthur Penny (both to win International cross-country honours later) and the brothers Jack and Joe Flower. Our seventh position earned us the special award medals. Joe Flower excelled himself in running the second fastest over stage 2, and placed us second at Mitcham. Even more improvement was shewn in 1930, when we finished fourth and earned a set of place medals. Our star runners were Allum, who did fastest time over his stretch and Syd Warboys, running for the first time who was second fastest on the long fifth stage of those days of 6 miles 352 yards. In the following year we actually finished fifth, but many thought our performance had more merit than that of the previous year. We suffered a bitter blow when Arthur Allum, having made four places in 2½ miles and seeming all set to peg back more, sustained an ankle injury and had to concede two of the places gained. Arthur had great difficulty in finishing and had to be carried away once the change-over had been effected. In this race another of our future Internationals, Tom Carter, made his debut. In 1932 the sporting papers advised the public that the Belgrave team had deteriorated and would not be in the first half-dozen - whereat we were secretly very pleased! The strongest field ever was promised; for all the leading clubs in the country were to be represented. Over the first eight stages we were either fourth or fifth - remarkable consistency. On the ninth relay yet another of our Internationals, that great character Bert Footer, showed his teeth and took us into third place, which was well held to the end by our Captain, Bill Webb. The two clubs to finish in front of us were Salford Harriers and Birchfield Harriers. Behind us were Aldershot Command A.C., South London Harriers and Surrey A.C. in that order, with fourteen other clubs following on. Every one of our runners set up a new Club record over his stage. Obviously the conditions must have been favourable, but here were ten magnificent performances. In those days we had on the road a double-decker bus, which served as grandstand and dressing room. The inside was curtained off and we actually dropped our man at his relay point, picked up our finishing runner and then passed through the field to the next change-over point and so on throughout the race. What a hopeless task it would be these days! Needless to say a very happy bus load of Belgravians returned to London on that day in April 1932. In 1933 third position was again ours, and Salford Harriers, from Manchester, and Birchfield Harriers were again in front of us.But once again we were the first Southern club home, and the future hope of the South to win a sporting victory over the Midlands and North. That came in 1934 - and how excited we were! April 14th was the date and the late Bill Rice was entrusted with the first stretch from Westminster and handed over third. Tom Carter held the position and next Harry Shields set about the opposition to some purpose. He quickly took the lead and also the baton carried by the leading team (the first Belgrave man to carry it). He still gripped it firmly and defiantly at Purley even though the Polytechnic Harriers runner got his nose in front in the last yard! Jack Flower (4th stage) had a three seconds lead over the Poly when handing over and 2 min. 2 sec. lead over Birchfield. Arthur Penny ran our fifth leg and finished 61 sec. ahead of the Poly with Birchfield nearly three minutes away; we were well on our way to our first victory! Syd Warboys increased our lead over the next stretch, and then we ran over successive stages two newcomers, Bert Shaw and Alf Taylor. Both ran well but nevertheless at Hickstead, Polytechnic and Birchfield had made some inroads into our lead. Bert Footer, on the Dale Hill stretch that he new so well, ran brilliantly, recording second best time over the stage to hand over nearly two minutes in front of Poly with Birchfield four minutes further back. Our great little International handed over to another of that gallant band, Arthur Allum, who sped on his way over the last stretch of 6 miles 904 yards to return the fastest for the stage, and gave us a winning margin of 2 mins. 6 sec. over Polytechnic Harriers, and 4 mins 9 secs. over Birchfield. Great was our delight! 1935 - we were now English Cross-country champions and holders of the Relay Trophy, the challenged, no longer the challengers. Birchfield Harriers tried all they knew to give us a beating and at the commencement of the last stage were only 17 seconds behind, but we ran out winners by 37 seconds. Newcomers to our team were Jim Ginty (one of our finest runners ever), Dan Patience and Syd Ring. Our hat-trick of wins was accomplished in 1936 and we were the first club to have three wins in a row, even though Birchfield could boast five wins in all. Two new boys in our team were Pat Parker and Ted Stimpson - both destined to become Cross-country Internationals. Our winning margin on this occasion was 13 seconds only from Birchfield - a most exciting race, marred only by the death of C. Young of Queens Park Harriers who was killed on the road. This was the first of the races to start from Mitcham and teams still consisted of ten men. 1937 was our Jubilee Year and naturally we wished to excel, but as so often happens at such times, we were doomed to disappointment. After taking the lead on the second relay (Pat Parker gained eight places) we held it all the way to Brighton and to within half a dozen yards of the tape, when Mitcham A.C. (represented by Dennis Brickwood, now well known as one of our members) managed to gain an inches win in almost the last stride! Birchfield were a mere 12 seconds behind us - what a race! Our team newcomers were Les Cohen and Bill Lucas, then a junior, but destined later to win Olympic and International honours. In 1938 we slipped back to third position, Mitcham A.C. again winning, with Birchfield second. Those were the days of mass unemployment, and many Welsh International runners were finding their way on to the nursing staff of a certain mental hospital in S.W. London, whence they became members of Mitcham A.C. Much high feeling was caused at the time, but one thing is certain, and that is that there were some grand runners and sportsmen among these Welsh runners. In our team for the first time were Len Herbert, due to become an International later, Harry Verney and Charlie Smart. Mitcham's hat-trick of wins was recorded in 1939 when we were second and Birchfield third. All our runners on this occasion had previous relay experience and one of the best performances was by Charlie Smart on the fifth leg. Then came War and it was "good-bye" to Brighton Relays until 1947. In our Diamond Jubilee Year we were again the winners, and in no uncertain manner, for we led on every stage except the eighth when we were second for a short while, but Len Herbert quickly took us to the fore again. Blackheath Harriers were second and Coventry Godiva third. Rather naturally there were new names in our team in Vic Blowfield, George Lucas, Stan Eales, Eric Herbert and Albert Frost. It is interesting to note that of our ten runners, six were past or future Internationals. Our 1948 win owed much to Bill Lucas who started the last lap 31 seconds behind Birchfield and passed the finishing line twenty seconds to the good! Newcomers to the team were Tom Clinton, Ken Stimpson, Martin Williamson and Eddie Short. Twenty-five clubs competed in 1949 and we accomplished our second hat-trick of wins, thus achieving more wins in the nineteen races held than any other club. Birchfield, Tipton and Reading A.C. finished 2nd, 3rd and 4th in that order. On April 1st 1950, old friends of ours for many years past on track and country, Thames Valley Harriers, scored their first win. It was definately not our day although we took the fourth set of medals, for Blackheath and Reading also anticipated us into Brighton. The first of the National Relays was staged in April 1951 over the Mitcham to Brighton course, and we were the winners from Thames Valley H. by nearly three minutes. Our team ran in this order:- C.W. Walker, L.W. Herbert, A. Bedford, W.E. Lucas, J.C. Smart, E. Herbert, J.W. Brown, J. Bromley, E. Short and L. Adams. The Southern Relay held later in the year provided us with another win - our fifth win in the last six races - and the minor places were filled by Blackheath H. and Polytechnic H. In 1952 Birchfield Harriers gained their first Relay win since 1931, beating us by 25 seconds with the Scottish Club, Victoria Park A.A.C. in third place. In this race Pete Newell made his debut, coming in as reserve on the fifth stage. He took us from tenth to fourth position and accomplished fastest time - what a reserve to have up one's sleeve! In the Southern Relay held later in the year we had yet another win by almost a minute from T.V.H.; Essex Beagles were third. Jack Brown, Arthur Bruce, Len Adams and Ray Tooby all broke stage records, with Eddie Short also doing so but finding one better runner on the day in Ken Norris of Thames Valley. The National Relay of 1953 found us slipping back to fourth place behind Thames Valley H., Birchfield H. and South London H. Bill Lucas recorded fastest time over the eighth stage. In the Southern Relay held in October we finished second to Essex Beagles with T.V.H. third. In 1954 the National Relay reverted to the old pre 1936 full length course from Westminster to Brighton (54¾). Our position was a meritorious second to South London Harriers with Essex Beagles third. Teams comprised eleven men and our team did exceedingly well although we were very conscious of the fact that five of our members were over 35 years of age, and of the need for some young replacements. The Southern Relay in October gave Herne Hill their first win with Thames Valley H. and ourselves second and third. We move more into the days of recent history and 1955 found us fourth in the National Relay behind S.L.H., Poly and Sheffield. The Southern Relay gave us a real shock - we were sixth! From 1932 onwards we had always won a set of medals in this event and now we were turned away empty. In 21 consecutive races we had been inside the first four places (on nine occasions, winners) and this is a record any club would be glad to have; but this fall from grace was all the harder! In 1956 we were fifth in the National event, S.L.H. winning for the third time in succession. We were happy to see two of our younger members Charlie Dabbs and George Flanagan performing so well. The Southern race gave us the chance of being in the "placings" once again, and we were third to Thames Valley H. and Herne Hill H. Jack Brown, as so often, ran splendidly for us. The 1957 National race also found us in third place, with S.L.H. winning once again. Ours was a satisfying performance. The Southern relay in October had added distance due to the re-laying of the road round Gatwick Airport, and twelve runners constituted a team. Thames Valley H. had an easy win but we took second place with Woodford Green A.C. third. As we were 18th at the end of the first relay we did well to come through to second at the end of the race. Last year we dropped to 11th in the National race and 6th in the Southern Relay. This year, as recorded elsewhere, we were placed 11th again in the National Relay; and in October we shall be able to try ourselves out once again with the other chosen clubs in the South. Our form in the last two years has borne no comparison with that of earlier days. It is true that many of our younger runners who by now should be establishing reputations in these relays have been prevented by injuries from turning out as regularly as we would have wished, but time is still on their side. In addition we have some excellent junior runners maturing and there can be little doubt that those golden days we enjoyed for so long can soon come back. But they will not return without plenty of purposeful hard work added to great enthusiasm and solid mutual team support in training, as well as in racing. These, we may be certain, will be forthcoming, and may we see their results soon! A.A.H. items.sum: Report of the Finchley 20 miles road race, with Belgrave winning the team race and the Belgrave finishers' positions and times.
items.s: FINCHLEY H. 20 MILES ROAD RACE - APRIL 18TH Report of the Finchley 20 miles road race, with Belgrave winning the team race and the Belgrave finishers' positions and times. This very popular event again attracted a large entry and there were actually 163 starters. Some tremendously fast running ensued and the winner (O'Gorman of St. Albans) covered the course in 1h.43m.26s.- 3m.25s. faster than the previous record. With such a fast winning time many meritorious performances "down the field" are apt to be overlooked, but Colin Collis deserves special mention for his 11th place in 1h.50m.50s as does Bob Plummer for his best ever time of 1h.52m.54s. In the team race we scored the same number of points as T.V.H. but our fourth scoring man finished ahead of two of their scoring members and so clinched first place. items.s: YOUR CLUB DINNER Notice of the club annual dinner on 14 November at Barrington House, with other social dates and Brighton Relay coach seats. Make a note of this date! NOVEMBER 14TH. Your attendance is requested at Barrington House, where our annual dinner is to be held. Here is your chance to meet all those members who, due to performing at different venues, you may not have seen during the season. Tickets are 22/6 and in the words of your Social Secretary "terms can be arranged". So come along and ensure that this is the best of all our dinners. Other social dates to note:- Oct.24th, Social Dance; Dec.5th, Social Dance; Jan.2nd, New Year's Dance; Jan.10th, Children's Party; Jan.23rd, Social Dance; Mar.19th, Social Dance; Lastly, do not forget the Brighton Relay on October 10th; coach seats can now be booked at 10/- each. items.s: MATCH v. HERCULES A.C. 13TH MAY. Report of the evening match against Hercules A.C., which began with the club 7 miles walk championship for the Frank Elson Cup, with the walk result. The evening commenced with the Club 7 miles walk Championship for the Frank Elson Cup. Notable absentees were Stan Vickers, the holder, and Eric Hall, last year's runner up. However, form had altered very little for Ray Hall, Hugh McGreechan and George Beecham, 3rd, 4th and 5th last year, filled the first three places this time in the same order! Although the turnout of Seniors and Juniors for the match with Hercules was quite good, they were outnumbered by the boys and youths present. Les Stokell and Tom Carter have a most enthusiastic bunch of youngsters under their wings; it gladdened one's heart to see so much promising young talent in Belgrave vests. A most exciting Senior 100 yds. was won by the versatile Charlie Jones in the good time of 10·2; Ron Holtum and S. Deane each clocked 10·3. The half-mile was notable for the last lap performance of John Thresher. With just over 500 yds. to go John was boxed in by a group of runners 12 yds. behind the leaders. Entering the back straight for the second time he made his effort to catch the leaders. Rubbery legs in the last 40 yds. prevented his doing so and Malcolm Robinson passed him on the line . However, he was undoubtedly the fastest over the second lap and its good to see him consistantly breaking 2 minutes these days. In the mile Derek Crookes gave a most welcome show of form by finishing third in a time of 4m.25·1s. Don Maclean also running well again did 4m.21s. and Alan Black 4m.25·7s. The standard in the long-jump was also high. Dave Ansell, runner up in the Sward Trophy a few days earlier could only manage 4th place this time with a similar distance! Jim McGrath, our new member from Northern Ireland who seems to be another Mal Ash, jumped a most creditable 21'0" to finish 5th. The junior sprints illustrated our sad lack of young sprinters but this was offset to some extent by the promising debut of Linley in the 440 yds. His time of 52·6s. should be cut considerably under the guidance of Frank Simmons, as he has the stamp of a class runner. Our junior Captain, Brian Kolbe performed creditably in both the 220 and 440 and is improving each time out. Eric Penny ran a very well judged race to win the mile in 4m.45·7s., an encouraging early season time. Result of 7 miles walk. 1, R.C. Hall 55.47; 2, R. Middleton 56.10; 3, G.S. items.sum: Report of the rushed evening match against H.H.H. and Q.P.H., with senior, junior and youths match scores.
items.s: MATCH v. H.H.H. & Q.P.H. MAY 20TH. Report of the rushed evening match against H.H.H. and Q.P.H., with senior, junior and youths match scores. Owing to a late start, and an already overcrowded programme for an evening meeting, the events had to be rushed through in double quick time; giving the appearance of some hybrid relay meeting. However this did not stop the athletes from putting up some good performances. Sylvan Deane won both the sprints in 10·5 and 22·8 and a now free from injury Gerry Leroy made a welcome comeback to win both second string sprints in 10·4 and 23·5 . Brian Morris and John Davies showed their class by cantering home in the 440 and 880 respectively and virtually clinched the match for us. An excellent start to the season was made by Norman Caves in the triple jump with 45'4", only 13" less than his highly ranked best of last year. Jim McGrath showed his versatility by adding the discus to his list of events, and continued his battle of the "half-inch" with Dave Ansell in the long jump. Jim and Dave seem to be inseparable in their long-jumping performances. In the junior match Brian Kolbe (2m.4·5s.) was our only winner although Eric Penny was narrowly beaten in the mile. The junior section must be hungrily awaiting the arrival of some of our promising youths. Les Stokell's lads did their duty in the youths match by beating Herne Hill. A few personalities will no doubt soon arise from their ranks and their progress watched with growing interest. Keep at it boys! items.label: No. 139
items.h: VANCOUVER TROPHY MEETING AT WOODFORD MAY 23RD
items.sum: Report of Belgrave's under-strength team at the Vancouver Trophy meeting staged by Woodford Green A.C. in a fierce wind.
items.s: VANCOUVER TROPHY MEETING AT WOODFORD MAY 23RD Report of Belgrave's under-strength team at the Vancouver Trophy meeting staged by Woodford Green A.C. in a fierce wind. This meeting was inaugurated in 1955 by Woodford Green A.C. to commemorate the performances of Elliott and Johnson in the previous year's Empire Games at Vancouver. The home club were virtually at full strength, but many athletes from some of the other clubs were conspicuous by their absence. Our own John Davies, Brian Morris, Clive Ryan, Frank Wright and D. McCorquindale were competing elsewhere, and with Stan Vickers Eric Hall, Norman Caves, Mal Ash and Andorka also unavailable our team could not be said to be truly representative of the name of Belgrave. Nevertheless, the lads who did carry our colours performed with considerable credit and had no small portion of bad luck. Conditions would have been ideal but for a fierce wind which affected almost every performance. Ron Holtum just failed to qualify for the final of the 100 m. recording 11·8 in his battle against both wind and competitors. In the 200m. we were out of luck again when S.Deane, who clocked 22·7s. was also unable to qualify. However, Dave Carter joined the finalists with a workmanlike performance a provided us with a very valuable point. In the 400m. C.Lindsay of Q.P.H. showed considerable speed and strength in negotiating the antics of the wind to record a phenomenal 47·7! How Brian Morris would have liked to have been there! Our own Alan Jackson (51·9) was also unable to reach the final but ran a sound race. When he has the courage to make his first 220 a little faster his times will undoubtedly improve. Dave Mitchell and John Thresher, both of whom are new arrivals to the senior ranks, each narrowly missed qualifying for the 800m final. They both ran very spirited races and in a couple of seasons time should prove to be outstanding performers. In the 1500m. Malcolm Robinson, our only entrant, found himself up against opponents such as Earl, Linford, Chapman and Ellis, but with his usual show of determination and ever-improving ability he secured a point with a time of 4m.2·4s., another best performance. In many events we were unable to field two competitors, which meant a possible wastage of points before we started. The 5000m. appeared to be another such event when a call was put out for the runners to assemble. Simultaneously, a certain Irishman, red-faced and panting, burst upon the scene having, seemingly, run a four minute mile from Woodford Station. Having had his clothes virtually dragged from him John Moore was ushered over to the starting line where he just had time to take a deep breath before travelling a further 5000 metres. John must be congratulated on his running although his performance, of course, was not one of his best. Don Maclean ran well in the first half of the race but when it became obvious that he wouldn't score he eased down to save himself for the steeplechase, in which he had volunteered to run. In the high hurdles Jim McGrath showed his prowess by qualifying for the final. Charlie did likewise in the 400m. hurdles and was a creditable fourth in 57·9s. Both Percy Porter and John Ware did well in finishing 3rd and 2nd in the hammer and javelin respectively. Jim McGrath led in the long jump until the final round where two competitors"pulled one out of the bag". Only 2¾" separated the first four! Both Jim and Dave Ansell, who was fourth, recorded 20'3", the wind accounting for a good two feet. Dave went on to a fourth place in the triple jump while Jim completed a "Mal Ash" type performance by finishing third in the pole vault, narrowly failing at 12'0", an excellent days work. Stan and Eric were sadly missed in the 3000m. walk, although Ted Smith and John Knifton gleaned a valuable three points between them. Prior to the 3000m steeplechase Clive Shippen paid the penalty of insufficient warming-up by pulling a thigh muscle when negotiating a hurdle. Thus Don Maclean faced yet another race as our sole competitor as this time there was no late arrival to join him. In doing 10.21 Don left behind several fresher opponents. As far as the match result was concerned Woodford Green were in an unassailable position quite early on. Of Belgrave's 32 points, 23 were obtained on the field and 9 on the track, from which you may form your own conclusions. C.S. items.s: R.W.A. 20 MILES ROAD WALK CHAMPIONSHIP - MAY 9TH Report of the R.W.A. 20 miles road walk championship at Imber Court, where Belgrave were second team and retained the Nijmegen Cup, with Belgrave positions and times. Held on a very hot day at Imber Court this race was notable for the way in which Tom Missen and Don Thompson, both of Metropolitan Walking Club, absolutely slaughtered the opposition. It was also notable for the performance of George Williams who came in at the last minute to replace Eric Hall, who had leg trouble. To finish fifth in such a class field at his first attempt over the distance deserves great praise. Credit must also be accorded to Terry Clark, only just out of the junior stage, for his very fine effort in finishing ninth. Although we lost the team race we did retain the Nijmegen Cup for the first club to finish eight men, indeed this is the fifth time in succession that we have won it. Teams:- 1st Met. items.sum: Report of the Surrey Championships at Motspur Park, at which Belgrave were represented in every event and swept the two miles walk, signed C.S.
items.s: SURREY CHAMPIONSHIPS - 29/30TH MAY. Report of the Surrey Championships at Motspur Park, at which Belgrave were represented in every event and swept the two miles walk, signed C.S. Without doubt Motspur Park has an atmosphere all of its own. A fast track in a pleasant, well-sheltered setting, together with a large appreciative crowd of spectators reclining on the grassy banks and the usually fine weather, make this meeting a rather special occasion for competitor and onlooker alike. A large proportion of the crowd consists of semi-retired athletes, still dabbling, who have not yet managed to resist the lure of an athletic meeting. At one time they would have returned home determined to make a "come back", but now, alas, the County Junior and Youth performances are sufficient cause to not only turn this group to full retirement but to swell their ranks by the addition of many more disillusioned Seniors. At Whitsun, Surrey's athletes allowed the Inter-County Trophy to slip across the river to their Middlesex rivals. But on thisday they made it quite clear that it had gone for no more than a year's holiday. Performances were improving all round but most noticeably amongst the younger competitors. Mitcham A.C. and Hercules A.C. were the most prominent but Belgrave were unique in being represented in every event - that is if one is allowed to count the announcer! Yes, Bill Lucas was on duty once more. Bill's announcing is second to none and he must be congratulated on the way he carried this marathon task. Highlights of the meeting were, a 1m.49·6s. "half" from Brian Hewson, a 48·7s. 440 by junior John Strachan of Hercules and a 13m.49·6s. conquest by his clubmate Ernie Earl over the redoubtable Mike Maynard in the three miles. For many this meeting started and finished on Friday evening, and no less dramatically than in the Senior mile heats. County standard is 4m.24s., yet Giddings of Deptford Park failed to qualify for the final with a time of 4m.13·7s.! and our own Malcolm Robinson likewise with a personal best of 4m.19s. In the two miles walk Belgrave swept to victory by filling the first three places; George Williams winning from Ray Middleton with John Knifton a good third in his first year of senior competition. On Saturday Clive Ryan and Charlie Jones comfortably qualified for the 440 final despite being drawn against each other in their heat and having to fill first two places. Clive recorded 49·9 and Charlie 51·0. In the final Clive was drawn on the outside lane, while the holder, Woodland of Hercules, was blessed with the inside. However, Woodland had to put up a Best Championship Performance of 48·4 in beating Clive's 49·4. Charlie was fifth in 51·3. Eric Penny ran well on Friday evening to qualify for the Junior mile final but found the opposition too strong next day. The first four broke the Best Championship Performance and the first seven were inside 4m.23s.! Harvey of Mitcham (4.16·8) led from start to finish to win from Harper of S.L.H. (4.19·1) Eric Shirley made his first appearance at the Championships and won the senior mile from A.S.Rogers of Mitcham in 4m.11s. - sixth man here clocked 4.14·4! Sylvan Deane (10·4) was narrowly beaten in his 100 yds. heat, being passed in the last ten yards in a blanket finish. The leading white-vested runner in the second heat of the 880 went by unrecognised as Belgravians cheered on Malcolm Robinson in the main bunch. When the first lap time of 54·8 was announced eyebrows were raised and on closer inspection it was seen to be Frank Wright. A barrage of voices carried Frank down the back straight and although caught in the final straight he qualified through second place in 1m.57·2s. - a good solo run. In the third heat John Thresher ran a personal best of 1.58·5. Belgrave's only representative in the three miles was Don Maclean who recorded 14m.57·8s., and as the crowd left was seen to be reclining against a post in the centre of the arena in a rather deflated state - a fitting end to the day. items.s: OTHER COUNTY CHAMPIONSHIPS Notes on Belgrave members at the Beds. and Hunts. and Middlesex county championships. P.C. Eldridge, in his first season back from overseas performed a most creditable treble in the Beds. and Hunts. Championships at Luton, winning the 100 in 10·2, the 220 in 22·8 and the 440 in 51·7. His return is most welcome and we look forward to his services in future trophy meetings. Norman Caves made the total four for Belgrave by yet again winning the triple jump with 43'6". In the Middlesex Championships at Enfield Dave Ansell was once more amongst the leading long jumpers and finished second with 21'5¼". John Davies, holder of the mile title, was unable to compete owing to other commitments. P.C. Eldridge P.C. Eldridge won 100 (10·2), 220 (22·8) and 440 (51·7) at Beds. and Hunts. items.s: EDITORIAL The new editors introduce themselves, explain this 28-page issue, and pick out Ray Hall, Peter Eldridge, Gerry LeRoy and Charlie Dabbs as performers to watch in Olympic year. Dear Fellow Members, This issue marks the arrival of a new Belgrave year, a new President, and as you can see from the head of this page - new Editors. We thank the Bishop brothers for helping to establish our journal as a regular, healthy and expressive organ of Club activity, and we will endeavour to maintain the high standards they have set. We hope to introduce new ideas in future issues and are quite prepared to face adverse criticism. A big post-bag indicates a lively readership, so let us have your ideas too. The Autumn issue of the Belgravian always has plenty of news to cover. This,together with a back-log of results to last June, has enabled us to produce the biggest issue for many years - 28 pages. We should hastily point out however, that for ecconomic reasons it is not possible to continue publishing more than 20 pages, so the accent will be on quality rather than quantity. Although the summer season was not one of our most succesful there emerged several performers who could well gain higher honours next year. In the forefront of these is Ray Hall who has been outstandingly consistent in his walking, and whose quest for Olympic honours will be followed with great interest. Peter Eldridge and Gerry LeRoy, in their first fully active season for some time, showed that very little lies between them and representative honours of high note, and Charlie Dabbs, who at long last triumphed over persistent injury and established himself as one of the country's leading distance runners by his magnificent performance in the R.R.C. 25km event. Success leads to success and as a result many other stars are likely to be swept along in the wake of these athletes. We are firmly of the opinion that Belgrave is now equipped with the right sort of material to commence a succession of highly successful seasons- and what better year to start than Olympic year, 1960! items.label: No. 140
items.sum: Profile of the newly elected President T.C. "Charlie" Jones, a member since 1926, covering his hurdling, field events, walking and administrative work.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT - 1959/60 Profile of the newly elected President T.C. "Charlie" Jones, a member since 1926, covering his hurdling, field events, walking and administrative work. Our newly-elected President, T.C."Charlie" Jones, has certainly grown-up with the Club for he became a member as far back as October,1926, and has been very much in evidence ever since in all our activities. His early interest in our sport was derived from his father who became a member on the Club's formation in 1887, and could tell many an interesting story of the early days; and of the matches Bels v Bats (the long-since defunct Battersea A.C.) on the roads over the Chelsea Bridge—Battersea Bridge circuit. Charlie was also a cricketer of some skill, and as junior and youth athletic events were infrequently held at the time, he spent most week-ends in perfecting his fast bowling. Despite his activities on the cricket pitch he was at all other times to be found at Battersea Park Track- the focal point of all our Summer interest in those days. The hurdles always fascinated Charlie and his first club award was for the event. Later he was to win the Surrey County 440 yards Hurdles Championships, and later still to gain Surrey County place medals in the Hop Step & Jump and Javelin Championships. He competed in our Junior Cross-country teams, and in later years established himself as one of our best runners at 440 and 880 yards. His long-striding action was a delight to watch, and only inability to translate that terrific stride into a sprint over the last thirty yards or so prevented him from carrying off many Championships. His interest has always been extended over the full range of field events, and he became a Club Champion at the triple jump and was responsible for many excellent performances in this event and the long-jump. To add to this story of athletic versatility must be added the fact that Charlie was always (and still is) a most accomplished stroller both at home and abroad; and had he decided to try himself out as a race-walker it is certain he would have achieved further successes. Charlie had the good fortune, shared with many others, to be part of that tremendous enthusiasm which permeated the Club in the late 1920's and 1930's, when our star was in the ascendant, when each month saw more battle honours won, more athletic history made. Even the slowest man in the Club felt he was pushing the man in front of him, who was forcing the man ahead of him to give of his best, and so up to Club team level when the reserves compelled the selected team men to run every inch of the way. Charlie epitomised this intense Club spirit and was at every Championship urging and working for our successes. On the administrative side Charlie has done yeoman work and served in a variety of offices and been in on higher councils for the greater part of his Club life. His legal knowledge has been of the greatest help to us, his especial work for Field Events and Coaching within the Club still continues; and his work in the administrative field has been almost as versatile as his active career in our colours. We may be sure that Charlie Jones will serve us well as President. Let us resolve to serve him and the Club equally as well. A.A.Harley. T.C. items.label: No. 140
items.sum: The new President thanks members for his election and calls for full teams and club spirit across all branches of the sport.
items.s: THE PRESIDENT SPEAKS The new President thanks members for his election and calls for full teams and club spirit across all branches of the sport. I view the bestowing upon me of the Presidency of this famous Club as the crowning glory of what seems almost a lifetime as a member. It comes to comparatively few and so is sure to be a treasured memory for the rest of my days. It came as the greatest surprise to know that I had even been considered for this honour. However having had it conferred upon me I would offer my sincere thanks and express my regrets that I was far away on holiday in Switzerland when the election took place. The latter however saved me the qualms of opening my mouth to verbally express my thanks. Enough of thanks, which I hope I have adequately expressed, and on to our aims as true Belgravians. We have a fine crowd of athletes in all branches of the sport in which we participate. We have our Internationals, and good,mediocre, and indifferent performers - rabbits as well. That is what a Club such as ours should have, it helps to make Athletics what it is. The burning spirit behind all and each should be "The Club" - to keep, to make and enhance its name and reputation. All can help in this - team spirit is what will achieve it. The turning out of full teams in all Championships,Competitions and even Club Matches should be the aim of everyone, even if it be only for the sake of not letting your Club mates down. We have had our successes in the past, but it is to the future we look, to repeat successes, achieve new ones and so to keep this great Club ever in the forefront of our sport. Being one of the few Clubs in the country which is so numerically strong in all its Branches -Track, Field, Cross-country, Road-running, Track and Road-walking - we have great opportunities and with your efforts doubled and re-doubled in the name of Belgrave successes must come. T.C.Jones The President. T.C. Jones T.C.Jones President Switzerland

items.s: KINNAIRD TROPHY - CHISWICK - JUNE 13th. Report of the Kinnaird Trophy at Chiswick, where Belgrave finished last of nine teams despite good track running. Although the final result proved to be our worst performance ever - last out of nine teams, our track men ran particularly well and were quite justified in feeling they had all the bad luck it was possible to have. The field event section were extremely weak and failed to collect a single point; most of the star performers being injured or committed elswhere. In the heats of the 100 yds. both Charle Jones and Sylvan Dean narrowly failed to qualify for the final with 10.1 and 10.4 secs respectively. Charlie, however, succeeded in the longer sprint with 22.3, whilst Peter Eldridge was eliminated with 22.2! Peter had previously missed qualifying for the 440 final by the finest of hairs breadths. With 50.2 Clive Ryan qualified for the final, but was unable to reproduce a similar time. With three to qualify in the 880 yards heats both John Thresher and Bob Taylor (Capt) finished fourth in their respective heats. John's time of 1:57.5 is a personal best . He is obviously a great prospect for the future. John Davies showed a most welcome return to form in the 1 mile turning the tables on Mal Robinson - his victor in the Club Champs., with 4:13.7 for 4th place, as against Mal's 4:19 for 9th. Yet another 4th place was recorded in the 3 miles where Pat Newell ran a creditable 14:23.8. Don Maclean was 12th in 15:23. 1.L.A.C. 50 pts. 2.T.V.H. 41 .. 3.WOODFORD GRN. A.C. 35 .. 9.BELGRAVE 9 .. items.s: MATCH v S.L.H. & ST.MARY'S COLLEGE TOOTING 17th JUNE. Report of a track match at Tooting against S.L.H., St. Mary's College and Ranelagh/Hermes, with Belgrave third among seniors and second among juniors. Brian Morris won the senior 'A' 220 in 23.8 whilst Alan Jackson secured second place in the 'B' with 23.6 - a grand start to the meeting. Dave Mitchell won a well judged quarter in the good time of 52.1 and Alan Black obtained further points by finishing 4th in the 880. Mal Robinson won an exciting mile in 4:23.2 after a ding-dong last lap struggle with Colin Wilson (S.L.H.). Ken Miller, making his first track apperance after foot trouble, did his fastest time to date finishing 4th in 4:32.6. As can be seen from the results, lack of depth in the team cost us the victory. However, an entertaining evening was concluded with Belgrave scoring their customary win in the relay. K.Blair and Bob Grant were 3rd and 5th respectively in the junior 100 yds. The former also did well in the 220, finishing 2nd ably supported by Dereck Wade, 4th, who is still a Youth. Bernard Linley, a great prospect, won the 440 in a canter from Mike Smithers, whilst our Junior Capt. Brian Kolbe was third in the 880 with 2:7.0 and Eric Penny 4th in the mile with 4:46.4. items.s: SOUTHERN SENIOR CHAMPIONSHIPS MOTSPUR PARK - JUNE 20th Belgrave performances at the Southern Senior Championships at Motspur Park, with a note on Peter Eldridge at the Midland Championships the same day. Brian Morris ran one of his best races of the season to record 48.4 secs to finish 3rd, behind Ted Sampson and Chris Lindsey who both clocked 47.7 secs. Pat Newell ran as consistently as ever to record a noteworthy 14:20 in the three miles. That time must now be Pat's average. Other good performances were made during the heats on Friday evening by Alan Jackson, with a 51.8 quarter and by Dave Mitchell (another fine prospect) who did a personal best of 1:56.6 in his 880 yds heat. John Davies was not at his best on this occasion and had to be content with a mile time of 4:16.8. The Midland Champs. were held on the same day with Peter Eldridge performing excellently in both the 220 and 440 yards. In the former event he finished 2nd to Robbie Brightwell of Birchfield in 22.0 secs and followed up with 3rd place in the 440, recording 50.7 secs - Well done, Peter! items.s: CECIL FRY TROPHY - WOODFORD - 4th JULY Report of the Cecil Fry Trophy at Woodford, where a weakened Belgrave team finished eighth, with Gerry LeRoy winning the quarter. Despite a strong wind to counter the 80 deg. temperature, the high humidity coupled with the loose state of the track made fast times impossible. This was not the only set-back, for we were minus all sprinters;they doing their best to record 2nd place behind the Valley, in the Southern 4 x 110 yards relay. It was therefore left to Gerry LeRoy to open our scoring. This he did with a vengance winning the quarter in a scintillating 49.4 secs. Alan Jackson was unable to reproduce the 51.8 he did in his heat and finished 6th, in 53.9 secs. Dereck Johnson ran as he liked to win the 880 yards, moving away from the field at 660, at which point our Dave Mitchell was lying second only to fade badly over the last furlong, and record 2:01 for 6th place. It was undoubtedly the heat which upset him, for as he said afterwards,"At 220 to go the heat hit me, and I folded up." Running his first track race this season for the Club, Ranjit Bhatia did well to close in at 9th with 4;23, in a good class mile. This was some three seconds faster and three places higher than Mal Robinson, who was however, running with a heavy cold. Our last track man Ray Middleton walked well to close-in fourth with 15:31.2 in the 2 mile walk. It was annoying to see only one field-events man but John Ware threw well to record fourth in the Javelin with 158'2½". 1. Ilford A.C. 47½ pts 2. Essex Beagles 40 .. =3. Cambridge/Woodford Grn. items.sum: Report of the Central Road Services Sports at Langley Park, with a close medley relay and Belgrave winning the 3 miles team award.
items.s: CEN. ROAD SERVICES SPORTS - 12th JULY Report of the Central Road Services Sports at Langley Park, with a close medley relay and Belgrave winning the 3 miles team award. We received an invitation to send a medley relay and a three mile team to this fixture, held on a grass track at Langley Park. In the medley relay only three teams turned out - T.V.H., Met. Police & Bels, so the boys were assured of ' a pot'. The first leg, an 880, was run by Dave Mitchell and he handed over to Alan Jackson some twenty yards behind Linford (T.V.H.) and Frank Wright, running for the Police. We lost a little further ground by the time Charlie Jones received the baton, and try as he could he was unable to make any impression on Dave Segal. With the quarter to go the Valley had some forty yards lead,with the Police twenty yards up on the Bels. It looked as if we were booked for third place. But Gerry LeRoy had other ideas! Running like a man inspired he had caught Brian Morris, running for the Police, by the 220 and was hareing after the Valley. With forty yards to go Gerry had caught and passed the Valley, but Morris with his customary last burst, moved up to pass on the line. A wonderful run Gerry!. Rangit Bhatia and Mal Robinson finished equal second in the 3 miles, after a desperate last 80 yards sprint. With half-a mile to go Anderson, the Police Champion, and Rangit moved away from Mal after the three had interchanged the lead all the way. When 300 yards out Mal began to sprint and had caught and had his nose in front by the home straight. But Rangit was not to be beaten and they crossed the line to-gether, with a time of 14:52.5, a personal best for each. Don Maclean and Charlie Walker finished 6th & 7th, for the team to take the team award. items.sum: Report of a small July match against Victoria Park at Battersea, which Belgrave won in the senior match and lost narrowly in the junior match.
items.s: MATCH v VICTORIA PARK - BATTERSEA - 15 JULY Report of a small July match against Victoria Park at Battersea, which Belgrave won in the senior match and lost narrowly in the junior match. July fixtures are not generally well supported, and this was by no means an exception. However, those present were equally divided between Vic.Pk. and ourselves, and a four-man field was found for most events; giving the match an International flavour! Victoria Park, noted for their middle-distance runners duly won the 880 and mile events, whereas the Bels scooped the 100, 220 and 440 yards. Gerry LeRoy won a sparkling 440 running in the out-side lane, and the ever versatile Jimmy Heathfield returned to the distance over which he was winning 12 years ago, to win the quarter in 54.6 secs. Following his now customary warm-up from dressing room to starting line Don Maclean duly took third place in the mile (after having borrowed some spikes) with a creditable 4:26.6. Norman Caves was in excellent form winning the high-jump with 584" and the hop-step & jump with 44'10". The ever present Jim McGrath was second to Norman in the high-jump, and also the shot, and it was most pleaseing to see Andorka competing once more after examinations, to win the shot with a putt of 43'1½". In the junior match Douglas Crosbie, our most promising sprinter who is but a youth, was narrowly beaten in the short sprint with 11.4, but ran a perfectly judged 220 to snatch victory in 24.2. Under the watchful eye of Frank Simmons he should become a most valuable addition to our senior sprint ranks. Bernard Linley, who will soon be knocking at the door of our senior teams, finished second in his first half-mile with 2:2.1, and soon after, over his favourite distance of 440 yards ran out a creditable winner in 54 .5 secs. The steadily improving Eric Penny was second in the mile with 4:38.1 followed by Brian Kolbe in 4:47.8. 1.BELGRAVE 37 pts 2.Vic.Pk. 23 .. Vic.Pk. 28 pts BELGRAVE 25 .. items.s: T.V.H. TRACK INTER-CLUB - ALPERTON - 18th JULY Report of the T.V.H. track inter-club at Alperton, highlighted by Gerry LeRoy's 440 win; Belgrave finished fourth. With two to run per event, we started the day with one entrant in the 100, Dave Carter. He, however, was quickly out of his blocks and qualified for the final quite comfortably. In the final he ran with plenty of fire and determination to come 4th in a good class field; Omagbi[illegible]i of T.V.H., being the winner. In the 220 Dave was again our only entrant, but Jimmy Heathfield filled the breach, and although he failed to qualify was by no means outclassed. Dave reached the final once more where he ran exceptionally well to finish a very good third behind Lindsey of Q.P.H. Both Gerry LeRoy and Charlie Jones qualified for the final of the quarter, despite Charlie feeling unwell owing to an attack of hay-fever. In the final, Gerry was drawn on the outside and Charlie in lane three;with Futter of University of London A.C., an AAA finalist the week previous. After two false starts the field got away particularly fast, with the wind behind them. At 220 Futter appeared to be slightly leading from Charlie with Gerry a close third. But with 220 to go Gerry made his effort which took him into the final straight level with Futter. Showing great fighting spirit into the powerful wind he gradually forged ahead to complete the most notable victory of the afternoon, in 49.4. Dave Mitchell and Dudley Gordon both reached the final of the 880 where Dave was narrowly beaten by Haith of the Valley. In the mile John Thresher ran particularly well to gain third place in 4:26.0 behind Pegley and Darchambaud (S.L.H.) 4:23.0 and finish in front of Mal Robinson. Don Maclean was our only scorer in the three miles, finishing fifth after gaining two places in the last lap; thus gaining two valuable points. Jimmy Heathfield had sportingly agreed to run but was forced to drop out after a mile. It was a pity we were unable to field a full relay for under the scoring of 12,10,8 etc., we were deprived of a second and possible first place in the Match. 1.T.V.H. 39 pts. 3.Q.P.H. 29 pts 2.S.L.H. 37 .. 4.BELGRAVE 28 .. items.s: BELGRAVE CLOSED MEETING - BATTERSEA - 22nd JULY Report of the club's closed meeting at Battersea, with Norman Caves winning the Charlie Cook Cup triple jump and Mal Robinson edging Pat Newell for the Griffen Cup three miles. Two Club Championships were included in the meeting and two worthy Champions emerged. In the "Charlie Cook Cup", Norman Caves was successful with a Triple Jump of 44'11½". Second was Charlie Jones (43'0½") whilst a newcomer of very great promise in A.Underwood jumped 42 ft. We shall watch his progress with the greatest of interest. The three mile Championships for the "Griffen Cup" brought out a full crop and a great race resulted. For lap after lap, Pat Newell, the holder, Mal Robinson, our Mile Champion, and Jim Radford ran together; neither giving nor expecting quarter. From the bell the first two named managed to struggle away from Jim; then Pat seemed to have the race well won when he opened up a lead of ten yards or so with only a furlong to go, but in the last few strides Mal got on terms and won by six inches both runners returning a time of 14:2 5. Well done both, and an especial word of congratulations to Jim Radford on an eye-opening performance which gives clear evidence that our younger element are going to take us right back where we belong. items.s: WOODFORD GREEN A.C. v ARMY v BELGRAVE - 8th AUG. Report of a three-way match with Woodford Green and the Army in which Belgrave finished third. The team approached this match in a light-hearted manner, now that the hurly-burly of the main competitions was behind them. Charlie Jones was the only one to survive in the sprints and went on to win the 220 yards with 22.4 secs. Out to prove himself our best quarter miler Gerry LeRoy streaked past the line to win with a time of 49.0 secs, with Alan Jackson 3rd, in a personal best 50.6 secs. The mile brought out our two most promising middle distance runners, Jim Radford and John Thresher. It was a good class field and it was to John's credit that he finished fourth in a personal best, 4:21.6. Jim found the last lap too fast and seemed a little disappointed with his 4:26.0 to gain sixth place - though this was yet another personal best. Beware; Davies, Bhatia and Robinson!!
